analysis.one_liner: Bars the SEC from requiring companies to disclose information not clearly material to investors.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have limited SEC disclosure rules, was introduced by two House Republicans and died in committee without any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped the Securities and Exchange Commission from imposing any new disclosure requirement on public companies unless the SEC first found a substantial likelihood that a reasonable investor would consider the information important to an investment decision [S2] [S3]. Notably, that restriction would apply only to adding rules — removing existing disclosure requirements would be exempt from the test [S3]. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on December 2, 2022, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Public companies and their executives would benefit most. They would face fewer mandatory disclosures to the SEC and lower compliance costs, because the SEC could only add a disclosure rule after expressly finding the information material to investors' decisions [S2] [S3]. Since removals are exempt from the same test, the bill also would have made it easier for future SECs to strip disclosure requirements than to add them [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Public companies would bear fewer SEC disclosure mandates, because the SEC could only impose a new disclosure requirement after expressly determining that a reasonable investor would consider the information important to an investment decision.
The restriction applies only to adding requirements, not removing them, so the bill would tilt the rulemaking process in favor of less disclosure for issuers.

analysis.who_pays: Investors — including ordinary workers whose retirement savings are invested in public companies — would bear the cost, getting less information about the companies they own. The materiality test could block SEC disclosure rules on matters like climate risk, cybersecurity, or workforce practices if the SEC could not show they matter to a typical investment decision [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: Investors would receive less information about the companies they own. The SEC could not require disclosure of any information it could not prove a reasonable investor would treat as important to an investment decision, which could block rules on matters such as climate risk, cybersecurity, or workforce practices that many investors say they want.

The bill is one-sided by design: its limit applies only to new disclosure requirements and explicitly exempts the removal of existing ones, so it would make stripping disclosure easier than adding it rather than applying a neutral standard.

Supporters' good-faith case — that SEC disclosure mandates had expanded beyond strictly investment-relevant information and that compliance costs fall on companies, especially smaller ones — would come at the price of leaving investors with a thinner information base for their decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to the public is minimal: lower compliance costs for public companies might save shareholders some money indirectly, but the bill's core effect is to restrict the information investors receive, and its asymmetric design (removals exempt from the test) favors less disclosure regardless of merit. What ordinary people would gain is small and indirect; what they would give up — information about the companies they invest in through pensions and mutual funds — is concrete. The bill was a low-stakes deregulatory measure that never advanced far enough for these trade-offs to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Huizenga introduced the bill on December 2, 2022, with Rep. Andy Barr as the only cosponsor, near the end of the two-year 117th Congress.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction; that was the last action ever taken on it.
The Democratic majority-controlled committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill never reached the House floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill would have written the legal 'materiality' test — the standard companies use in court to challenge disclosure rules — into statute as a precondition for any new SEC disclosure requirement.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Investors, including workers with retirement savings, are better off because the bill died: the SEC's existing authority to require disclosure from public companies remained intact, and public companies did not get the statutory limit on new disclosure rules they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Investors and the SEC's disclosure authority

for.name: Rep. Bill Huizenga
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 2, 2022, to limit SEC disclosure rulemaking to material information.

for.name: Rep. Andy Barr
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; he was its only cosponsor.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee (Democratic majority)
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No committee or floor vote ever occurred, so no one's position was tested; the only sponsorship came from two House Republicans, with no Democratic support on record.

industries.note: The bill would have capped the SEC's power to add disclosure requirements, cutting public companies' compliance costs and shielding them from rules on matters the SEC could not prove material to investment decisions. Their gain comes directly out of the information available to the investors who own them.

Funds and asset managers that research and steward companies on behalf of savers rely on SEC-mandated disclosures. A statutory materiality gate could have deprived them of data on emerging risks, making it harder to evaluate the companies their clients own.
